reg.ae-csl.name: UAE Cybersecurity Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 34 of 2021)
reg.ae-csl.summary: The UAE Cybersecurity Law establishes a comprehensive legal framework for protecting information systems, networks, and data across the UAE. Enforced by the UAE Cybersecurity Council, it criminalizes unauthorized access, data breaches, and cyberattacks, while mandating cybersecurity measures for government entities and critical infrastructure operators.
reg.ae-csl.req.1: Protection of government information systems, networks, databases, and IT infrastructure
reg.ae-csl.req.2: Criminalization of unauthorized access to information systems and electronic data
reg.ae-csl.req.3: Mandatory cybersecurity measures for entities handling sensitive government data
reg.ae-csl.req.4: UAE Cybersecurity Council oversight and coordination of national cybersecurity strategy
reg.ae-csl.req.5: Incident response coordination through the national Computer Emergency Response Team (aeCERT)
reg.ae-csl.req.6: Regulation of cybersecurity service providers and penetration testing activities
reg.ae-csl.penalties: Imprisonment of 1 to 15 years depending on offence severity. Fines ranging from AED 100,000 to AED 3 million. Deportation for non-citizens. Aggravated penalties for attacks on critical infrastructure, government systems, or systems affecting national security.
reg.ae-pdpl.name: Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data (PDPL)
reg.ae-pdpl.summary: The UAE's first federal-level data protection law establishes a framework for the protection of personal data. It applies to data controllers and processors operating within the UAE, excluding DIFC and ADGM free zones which have their own data protection regimes. Executive regulations for full enforcement details are pending.
reg.ae-pdpl.req.1: Obtain consent before processing personal data (with limited exceptions)
reg.ae-pdpl.req.2: Provide transparent privacy notices to data subjects
reg.ae-pdpl.req.3: Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
reg.ae-pdpl.req.4: Appoint a Data Protection Officer where required
reg.ae-pdpl.req.5: Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing
reg.ae-pdpl.req.6: Restrict cross-border data transfers to adequate jurisdictions or with safeguards
reg.ae-pdpl.req.7: Respond to data subject rights requests (access, correction, erasure, portability)
reg.ae-pdpl.penalties: Indicative administrative fines of AED 50,000 to AED 5,000,000 (formal penalty structure pending executive regulations). Criminal penalties under parallel law include at least AED 20,000 fine and up to 1 year imprisonment for unlawful data disclosure. Enforced by the UAE Data Office.
reg.ar-pdpa.name: Personal Data Protection Act (Ley 25.326)
reg.ar-pdpa.summary: Argentina's comprehensive data protection law was one of the earliest in Latin America, leading to an EU adequacy determination in 2003. It regulates the processing of personal data in both public and private databases, granting individuals habeas data rights.
reg.ar-pdpa.req.1: Obtain free, express, and informed consent before processing personal data
reg.ar-pdpa.req.2: Register databases with the national registry (AAIP)
reg.ar-pdpa.req.3: Implement adequate security and confidentiality measures
reg.ar-pdpa.req.4: Respect data subject rights (access, rectification, suppression, opposition)
reg.ar-pdpa.req.5: Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
reg.ar-pdpa.req.6: Limit data collection to what is relevant and not excessive
reg.ar-pdpa.req.7: Ensure data quality, accuracy, and currency
reg.ar-pdpa.penalties: Administrative fines from ARS 1,000 to ARS 100,000. Additional sanctions include database suspension or closure. Criminal penalties: 1 month to 3 years imprisonment for knowingly inserting false data. Enforced by the Agencia de Acceso a la Informacion Publica (AAIP).
reg.au-aml-ctf.name: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
reg.au-aml-ctf.summary: Australia's AML/CTF Act establishes a regulatory framework to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing. Administered by AUSTRAC, it imposes customer identification, reporting, and record-keeping obligations on reporting entities across financial services, gambling, bullion dealing, and designated services sectors.
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.1: Customer identification and verification (Know Your Customer/KYC) before providing designated services
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.2: Ongoing customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.3: Suspicious matter reporting (SMRs) to AUSTRAC for suspected money laundering or terrorism financing
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.4: Threshold transaction reports for cash transactions of AUD 10,000 or more
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.6: AML/CTF programs with Part A (customer identification) and Part B (employee due diligence) components
reg.au-aml-ctf.req.7: Record-keeping requirements for 7 years after the end of the customer relationship
reg.au-aml-ctf.penalties: Civil penalties up to AUD 22.2 million per contravention for reporting entities. Criminal penalties including imprisonment for tipping off or structuring offences. AUSTRAC may issue infringement notices, enforceable undertakings, and remedial directions.
reg.au-privacy-act.name: Privacy Act 1988 (as amended 2024)
reg.au-privacy-act.summary: Australia's primary federal privacy legislation, substantially amended in December 2024. It establishes 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) governing how organizations handle personal information, with a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy and dramatically increased penalties.
reg.au-privacy-act.req.1: Comply with 13 Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) covering collection, use, disclosure, and storage
reg.au-privacy-act.req.2: Mandatory data breach notification to the OAIC and affected individuals for eligible breaches
reg.au-privacy-act.req.3: Publish a clear and up-to-date privacy policy
reg.au-privacy-act.req.4: Provide individuals with access to and correction of their personal information
reg.au-privacy-act.req.5: Take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse, loss, and unauthorized access
reg.au-privacy-act.req.6: Only collect personal information that is reasonably necessary for organizational functions
reg.au-privacy-act.penalties: Maximum penalty for serious or repeated breaches: the greater of AUD 50 million, three times the benefit obtained, or 30% of adjusted turnover. Mid-tier penalties of AUD 3.3 million for bodies corporate. Enforced by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).
reg.au-soci.name: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (SOCI Act)
reg.au-soci.summary: Australia's SOCI Act establishes a regulatory framework to manage risks to critical infrastructure across 11 sectors. Significantly expanded in 2021-2022, it introduced mandatory cyber incident reporting, critical infrastructure risk management programs, and government assistance powers for responding to serious cyber incidents.
reg.au-soci.req.1: Critical infrastructure risk management programs covering cyber, physical, personnel, and supply chain risks
reg.au-soci.req.2: Mandatory reporting of critical cyber security incidents to the Australian Cyber Security Centre within 12 hours
reg.au-soci.req.3: Reporting of other cyber security incidents within 72 hours
reg.au-soci.req.4: Systems of National Significance subject to enhanced obligations including incident response planning
reg.au-soci.req.5: Government assistance measures allowing ASD to intervene during serious cyber incidents
reg.au-soci.req.6: Covers 11 sectors: communications, data storage, energy, financial services, food, health, higher education, space, transport, water, defence
reg.au-soci.penalties: Civil penalties up to AUD 55,500 per contravention for failure to comply with risk management obligations. Fines up to AUD 11,100 for failure to report cyber incidents. Government assistance provisions allow mandatory directions during imminent threats.
reg.bd-dsa.name: Bangladesh Data Protection Act 2023
reg.bd-dsa.summary: Bangladesh's Data Protection Act establishes the country's first dedicated data protection framework. It regulates the processing of personal and sensitive personal data, creates the Office of the Data Protection Officer, and sets requirements for consent, data breach notification, and cross-border transfers applicable to both public and private sector entities.
reg.bd-dsa.req.1: Consent required for processing personal data with specified lawful basis exceptions
reg.bd-dsa.req.2: Special protections for sensitive personal data including biometric, health, and financial data
reg.bd-dsa.req.3: Data breach notification to the Data Protection Office within 72 hours
reg.bd-dsa.req.4: Cross-border data transfer restrictions requiring adequate protection in the receiving country
reg.bd-dsa.req.5: Individual rights to access, correction, and erasure of personal data
reg.bd-dsa.req.6: Office of the Data Protection Officer established as the national supervisory authority
reg.bd-dsa.penalties: Fines up to BDT 25 lakh (2.5 million) for non-compliance. Higher penalties for repeat violations. The Data Protection Office may issue compliance orders, conduct investigations, and impose administrative sanctions.
reg.bh-pdpl.name: Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 30 of 2018)
reg.bh-pdpl.summary: Bahrain's first comprehensive data protection law regulates the collection, processing, and use of personal data by both public and private sector entities. It establishes individual rights similar to the GDPR, including rights to access, rectification, erasure, and objection to automated decision-making.
reg.bh-pdpl.req.1: Obtain consent before processing personal data
reg.bh-pdpl.req.2: Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
reg.bh-pdpl.req.3: Notify the authority of data breaches
reg.bh-pdpl.req.4: Restrict cross-border transfers to countries on the authority's approved list
reg.bh-pdpl.req.5: Respect data subject rights (access, rectification, deletion, objection)
reg.bh-pdpl.req.6: Register data processing activities with the Personal Data Protection Authority
reg.bh-pdpl.penalties: Criminal penalties: imprisonment up to 1 year and/or fine from BHD 1,000 to BHD 20,000. Administrative fines up to BHD 20,000, plus daily penalties up to BHD 1,000 for ongoing violations. Fines may be doubled for corporate entities and repeat offenses. Enforced by the Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA).
reg.br-ai-act.name: Brazil Artificial Intelligence Act (PL 2338/2023)
reg.br-ai-act.summary: Brazil's AI Act establishes a comprehensive risk-based regulatory framework for artificial intelligence systems. Approved by the Senate in December 2024, it classifies AI systems into risk tiers, mandates algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk applications, creates a national AI governance authority, and applies extraterritorially to AI systems whose effects reach Brazil.
reg.br-ai-act.req.1: Risk-based classification: minimal, high, and excessive risk AI systems
reg.br-ai-act.req.2: Prohibited AI practices including social scoring and subliminal manipulation
reg.br-ai-act.req.3: Algorithmic impact assessments required for high-risk AI systems
reg.br-ai-act.req.4: Transparency requirements including disclosure when individuals interact with AI systems
reg.br-ai-act.req.5: Human oversight mechanisms for high-risk AI decision-making
reg.br-ai-act.req.6: National AI governance authority for oversight, registration, and enforcement
reg.br-ai-act.req.7: Extraterritorial application to AI systems producing effects in Brazil
reg.br-ai-act.penalties: Fines up to 2% of annual revenue in Brazil or BRL 50 million per violation, whichever is greater. Temporary or permanent suspension of AI system operations. Public disclosure of violations and prohibition of processing certain data types.
reg.br-cncs.name: Brazil National Cybersecurity Policy (Decree No. 11,856/2023)
reg.br-cncs.summary: Brazil's National Cybersecurity Policy establishes the strategic framework for protecting cyberspace and digital infrastructure across the country. It creates the National Cybersecurity Committee (CNCiber) to coordinate policy implementation, promote public-private collaboration, and develop cybersecurity capabilities for government and critical infrastructure sectors.
reg.br-cncs.req.1: National Cybersecurity Committee (CNCiber) established for policy coordination and oversight
reg.br-cncs.req.2: Cybersecurity standards and guidelines for federal government information systems
reg.br-cncs.req.3: Critical infrastructure protection framework across energy, telecommunications, and financial sectors
reg.br-cncs.req.4: National cybersecurity incident response coordination through CERT.br and CTIR Gov
reg.br-cncs.req.5: Promotion of cybersecurity education, workforce development, and research
reg.br-cncs.req.6: International cooperation on cybersecurity threats and information sharing
reg.br-cncs.penalties: The decree establishes policy framework rather than direct penalties. Enforcement is through sector-specific regulators. Federal agencies must comply with cybersecurity directives or face administrative accountability measures. Critical infrastructure non-compliance addressed through existing regulatory frameworks.
reg.br-lgpd.name: Lei Geral de Protecao de Dados (LGPD)
reg.br-lgpd.summary: Brazil's General Data Protection Law is modeled after the EU GDPR and establishes comprehensive rules for the collection, use, processing, and storage of personal data. The ANPD (National Data Protection Authority) oversees enforcement and regulation.
reg.br-lgpd.req.1: Ten legal bases for processing personal data (including consent and legitimate interest)
reg.br-lgpd.req.2: Data subject rights including access, correction, deletion, and portability
reg.br-lgpd.req.4: Data processing records must be maintained
reg.br-lgpd.req.5: Cross-border data transfer restrictions with adequacy requirements
reg.br-lgpd.req.6: Privacy impact assessments for high-risk processing activities
reg.br-lgpd.req.7: Breach notification to the ANPD within a reasonable timeframe
reg.br-lgpd.penalties: Up to 2% of revenue in Brazil, capped at BRL 50 million per violation.
reg.ca-ab-hia.name: Alberta Health Information Act (HIA)
reg.ca-ab-hia.summary: Alberta's health privacy law governing how custodians and their affiliates collect, use, disclose, and protect individually identifying health information in the publicly funded health system. Private-sector organizations that are not custodians remain under Alberta's PIPA.
reg.ca-ab-hia.scope: Custodians under the Act — including physicians, pharmacists and other designated health professionals, Alberta Health Services, and Alberta Health — plus their affiliates, such as employees, contractors, and information managers that process health information for them.
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.1: Collect, use, and disclose only the health information essential for the intended purpose, at the highest degree of anonymity possible
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.2: Prepare a privacy impact assessment and submit it to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta before implementing new practices or information systems that collect, use, or disclose health information
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.3: Protect health information with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.4: Notify the Commissioner, the Minister of Health, and the affected individual as soon as practicable of a loss or unauthorized access or disclosure that poses a risk of harm
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.5: Affiliates must report breaches to their custodian
reg.ca-ab-hia.req.6: Give individuals access to and correction of their health information
reg.ca-ab-hia.penalties: Offence fines up to $200,000 CAD for individuals and $1,000,000 CAD for any other person. Enforced by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta.
reg.ca-ab-pipa.name: Alberta Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA)
reg.ca-ab-pipa.summary: Alberta's private-sector privacy legislation, deemed substantially similar to PIPEDA by the federal government. It governs how private-sector organizations in Alberta collect, use, and disclose personal information, including employee personal information, and applies to provincially regulated organizations operating within the province.
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.1: Obtain consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.2: Collect only the personal information reasonably necessary for the stated purpose
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.3: Provide individuals access to their personal information and the right to request corrections
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.4: Protect personal information with reasonable security safeguards
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.5: Designate a privacy officer responsible for compliance
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.6: Notify the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta without unreasonable delay of any breach posing a real risk of significant harm; notify affected individuals when the Commissioner requires it
reg.ca-ab-pipa.req.7: Collect, use, and disclose employee personal information only as reasonably required to establish, manage, or end the employment relationship
reg.ca-ab-pipa.penalties: Fines up to $10,000 CAD for individuals and $100,000 CAD for organizations per offense, including for failing to notify the Commissioner of a breach. Enforced by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta. No private right of action.
reg.ca-bc-pipa.name: British Columbia Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA)
reg.ca-bc-pipa.summary: British Columbia's private-sector privacy legislation, deemed substantially similar to PIPEDA. It governs how private-sector organizations in BC collect, use, and disclose personal information, including employee personal information, and it covers BC provincial political parties. Federal political parties are exempt from provincial privacy laws under a 2026 amendment to the Canada Elections Act. Unlike PIPEDA and Alberta's PIPA, it imposes no mandatory breach-notification duty.
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.1: Obtain consent appropriate to the sensitivity of the personal information
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.2: Collect personal information only for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.3: Allow individuals to access and request correction of their personal information
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.4: Make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal information against unauthorized access, use, disclosure, or loss
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.5: Designate a person responsible for the organization's compliance and make their title and contact information available
reg.ca-bc-pipa.req.6: Collect, use, and disclose employee personal information only as reasonable to establish, manage, or end the employment relationship, with notice to the employee
reg.ca-bc-pipa.penalties: Fines up to $10,000 CAD for individuals and $100,000 CAD for organizations per offense. Enforced by the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia. No private right of action.
reg.ca-cccs.name: Canada Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act
reg.ca-cccs.summary: Canada's Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act (CCSPA) establishes a cybersecurity framework for designated operators of federally regulated critical infrastructure. It was enacted by Bill C-8 (S.C. 2026, c. 9), which received Royal Assent on 15 June 2026, after its predecessor Bill C-26 died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025. The Act comes into force on dates fixed by order of the Governor in Council, and no such order had been made as of October 2026, so it is not yet in force and no operator classes have been designated. Not to be confused with the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act (CCPSA).
reg.ca-cccs.req.1: Designated operators must establish a cybersecurity program within 90 days of designation, file it with their regulator, and review it annually
reg.ca-cccs.req.2: Identify and mitigate cybersecurity risks in the supply chain and from third-party products and services
reg.ca-cccs.req.3: Report cybersecurity incidents to the Communications Security Establishment within the prescribed period, not exceeding 72 hours, and notify the regulator
reg.ca-cccs.req.4: Comply with cybersecurity directions issued by the Governor in Council
reg.ca-cccs.req.5: Keep records of the cybersecurity program, incidents, supply-chain mitigation, and directions in Canada
reg.ca-cccs.req.6: Covers federally regulated sectors: telecommunications, finance, energy, and transportation
reg.ca-cccs.penalties: Administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 500,000 per violation for individuals and CAD 15 million for any other person. Offences carry fines at the court's discretion and, for individuals convicted on indictment, up to 5 years imprisonment; each day of a continuing violation is a separate offence. Compliance orders and injunctions.
reg.ca-ccpsa.name: Canada Consumer Product Safety Act
reg.ca-ccpsa.summary: Canada's federal consumer product safety law, enacted by Bill C-36 (S.C. 2010, c. 21), governing consumer products that are manufactured, imported, advertised, or sold in Canada. It prohibits products that pose a danger to human health or safety, requires incident reporting and traceability, and lets Health Canada order tests, corrective measures, and recalls. Not to be confused with the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act (CCSPA).
reg.ca-ccpsa.req.1: Do not manufacture, import, advertise, or sell a consumer product that is a danger to human health or safety, or that is subject to a recall order
reg.ca-ccpsa.req.2: Report incidents, defects, or recalls in another jurisdiction to Health Canada within 2 days of becoming aware of them, and file a written report within 10 days
reg.ca-ccpsa.req.3: Keep documents identifying where products were obtained and to whom they were sold, for 6 years
reg.ca-ccpsa.req.4: Comply with Health Canada orders to test or study a product and to provide the results
reg.ca-ccpsa.req.5: Comply with recall orders and other corrective-measure orders
reg.ca-ccpsa.penalties: On indictment, fines up to $5,000,000 CAD and up to 2 years imprisonment; on summary conviction, up to $250,000 CAD for a first offence and $500,000 CAD thereafter. Knowing or reckless contraventions carry a fine at the court's discretion and up to 5 years imprisonment. Administrative monetary penalties up to $25,000 CAD per violation for commercial violators. Directors and officers can be personally liable.
reg.ca-mdr.name: Health Canada Medical Devices Regulations (SOR/98-282)
reg.ca-mdr.summary: Canada's federal regulations, made under the Food and Drugs Act, governing the sale, import, and advertising of medical devices, including software as a medical device. Devices are classified by risk from Class I to Class IV, and Health Canada licenses devices and the establishments that import or distribute them, and oversees post-market safety.
reg.ca-mdr.req.1: Classify each device by risk (Class I lowest to Class IV highest); a device that fits two classes takes the higher
reg.ca-mdr.req.2: Hold a medical device licence before importing or selling a Class II, III, or IV device
reg.ca-mdr.req.3: Hold a medical device establishment licence to import or distribute devices, unless an exemption applies
reg.ca-mdr.req.4: Report incidents involving death or serious deterioration in health within 10 days, and incidents that could cause it if they recurred within 30 days
reg.ca-mdr.req.5: Notify the Minister within 24 hours of deciding to recall a device, and report on the recall's results
reg.ca-mdr.req.6: Report serious risks identified in foreign actions within 72 hours, and prepare annual or biennial summary reports for Class II to IV devices
reg.ca-mdr.req.7: Address cybersecurity in pre-market applications for connected devices, per Health Canada guidance
reg.ca-mdr.penalties: Under the Food and Drugs Act: on indictment, fines up to $5,000,000 CAD and up to 2 years imprisonment; on summary conviction, up to $250,000 CAD and 6 months for a first offence and $500,000 CAD and 18 months thereafter. Knowingly or recklessly causing a serious risk of injury carries a fine at the court's discretion and up to 5 years imprisonment. Each day of a continuing offence is a separate offence.
reg.ca-on-phipa.name: Ontario Personal Health Information Protection Act (PHIPA)
reg.ca-on-phipa.summary: Ontario's health privacy law governing how health information custodians collect, use, and disclose personal health information, and how their agents and service providers handle it on their behalf. It sits alongside PIPEDA and has been declared substantially similar to it for custodians, so PHIPA rather than PIPEDA governs health information they handle in Ontario.
reg.ca-on-phipa.scope: Health information custodians in Ontario — physicians, hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, long-term care homes, and similar providers — plus their agents and the electronic service providers that handle personal health information for them, including health-tech vendors.
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.1: Obtain consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of personal health information, express or implied within the circle of care
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.2: Take reasonable steps to protect personal health information against theft, loss, and unauthorized use or disclosure
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.3: Notify the affected individual at the first reasonable opportunity of any theft, loss, or unauthorized use or disclosure
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.4: Report prescribed privacy breaches, such as theft, intentional misuse, or a pattern of breaches, to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, and file annual breach statistics
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.5: Give individuals access to and correction of their health records
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.6: Designate a contact person and publish a written statement of information practices
reg.ca-on-phipa.req.7: Agents and electronic service providers may use personal health information only as the custodian permits
reg.ca-on-phipa.penalties: Offence fines up to $200,000 CAD and up to one year imprisonment for individuals, and up to $1,000,000 CAD for organizations. Administrative monetary penalties from the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario of up to $50,000 CAD for individuals and $500,000 CAD for organizations, plus any economic benefit gained from the contravention.
reg.ca-pipeda.name: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)
reg.ca-pipeda.summary: Canada's federal private-sector privacy law governing how commercial organizations collect, use, and disclose personal information in the course of for-profit activities. PIPEDA applies across all provinces for federally regulated industries and in provinces without substantially similar legislation.
reg.ca-pipeda.req.1: Obtain meaningful consent for the collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
reg.ca-pipeda.req.2: Limit collection to purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate
reg.ca-pipeda.req.3: Provide individuals with access to their personal information upon request
reg.ca-pipeda.req.4: Allow individuals to challenge the accuracy and completeness of their data
reg.ca-pipeda.req.5: Protect personal information with safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity
reg.ca-pipeda.req.6: Appoint a privacy officer accountable for the organization's compliance
reg.ca-pipeda.req.7: Mandatory breach reporting to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals
reg.ca-pipeda.penalties: Up to $100,000 CAD per violation for offenses such as obstructing investigations, retaliating against whistleblowers, or failing to report breaches. Enforced by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.
reg.ca-qc-hssia.name: Quebec Act respecting health and social services information
reg.ca-qc-hssia.summary: Quebec's dedicated health privacy law, enacted by Bill 3 in 2023, governing health and social services information held by public and private bodies in the health and social services sector. It takes this information out of Quebec's general public- and private-sector privacy laws, including Law 25, and creates its own regime for access, protection, and incident reporting.
reg.ca-qc-hssia.scope: Health and social services bodies in Quebec — public institutions, private clinics and medical offices, pharmacies, laboratories, private seniors' residences, and other designated providers — and the third parties that hold or process their information under contract.
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.1: Collect, use, and communicate health and social services information only as the Act permits, with consent for uses outside the care relationship
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.2: Report confidentiality incidents that present a risk of serious injury to the Minister of Health and Social Services and the Commission d'accès à l'information, and notify affected individuals
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.3: Keep a register of all confidentiality incidents
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.4: Adopt governance rules and security measures for the information, and log access to it
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.5: Give individuals access to their information and let them restrict who can access it
reg.ca-qc-hssia.req.6: Contractors holding the information must meet the same protection obligations as the body they serve
reg.ca-qc-hssia.penalties: Penal fines of $1,000–$10,000 CAD for individuals and $3,000–$30,000 CAD for organizations for offences such as failing to report a confidentiality incident, and $5,000–$100,000 CAD for individuals and $15,000–$150,000 CAD for organizations for serious offences such as unauthorized access or communication. Fines double for a second offence and triple thereafter. Enforced by the Commission d'accès à l'information; there are no administrative monetary penalties.
reg.ca-qc-law25.name: Quebec Law 25 (Act Respecting the Protection of Personal Information in the Private Sector)
reg.ca-qc-law25.summary: Quebec's comprehensive modernization of its private-sector privacy framework, introducing GDPR-style requirements in three phases completed by September 2024. It applies to all organizations collecting, holding, or using personal information of Quebec residents, regardless of where the organization is based.
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.1: Designate a person responsible for the protection of personal information
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.2: Mandatory privacy impact assessments for information systems and electronic service delivery
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.3: Breach notification to the Commission d'acces a l'information and affected individuals
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.4: Right to data portability in a commonly used technological format
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.5: Express consent required for the collection of sensitive personal information
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.6: Privacy by default for technology products and services
reg.ca-qc-law25.req.7: Restrictions on profiling and automated decision-making with right to explanation
reg.ca-qc-law25.penalties: Administrative monetary penalties up to $10 million CAD or 2% of worldwide turnover. Penal fines up to $25 million CAD or 4% of worldwide turnover for serious offenses. Private right of action for individuals.
reg.ch-fadp.name: Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP / nFADP)
reg.ch-fadp.summary: Switzerland's revised Federal Act on Data Protection replaced the 1992 law to align more closely with the EU GDPR. It applies to the processing of personal data of natural persons by private persons and federal bodies, including organizations outside Switzerland processing Swiss residents' data.
reg.ch-fadp.req.2: Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing
reg.ch-fadp.req.3: Notify the FDPIC of data security breaches as soon as possible
reg.ch-fadp.req.4: Obtain opt-in consent for processing of sensitive personal data
reg.ch-fadp.req.5: Provide transparent privacy notices to data subjects
reg.ch-fadp.req.6: Ensure adequate protection for cross-border data transfers
reg.ch-fadp.req.7: Implement privacy by design and privacy by default
reg.ch-fadp.penalties: Maximum fine of CHF 250,000 (~EUR 263,000) against responsible individuals for intentional serious violations. Companies may be fined up to CHF 50,000 if identifying the responsible individual would require disproportionate effort. Enforced by the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC).
reg.cl-law19628.name: Law 19.628 on the Protection of Private Life (Ley sobre Proteccion de la Vida Privada)
reg.cl-law19628.summary: Chile's current data protection law, enacted in 1999, was one of the first in Latin America. It regulates the processing of personal data in public and private databases. A comprehensive replacement (Law 21.719) was enacted in December 2024 but does not enter into force until December 2026.
reg.cl-law19628.req.1: Obtain consent of the data holder for the processing of personal data
reg.cl-law19628.req.2: Process personal data only for purposes for which it was collected
reg.cl-law19628.req.3: Ensure data accuracy and update or delete inaccurate data
reg.cl-law19628.req.4: Respect data subject rights (access, rectification, cancellation, objection)
reg.cl-law19628.req.5: Restrict collection of sensitive data without explicit legal basis
reg.cl-law19628.req.6: Publish transparency requirements for public databases
reg.cl-law19628.penalties: Civil liability for damages caused by improper data processing. No dedicated enforcement authority or administrative fines under the current law. Courts handle complaints directly. The upcoming Law 21.719 (effective December 2026) will create a dedicated agency with administrative fining powers.
reg.cl-ley21719.name: Chile Law 21.719 on the Protection of Personal Data (Ley 21.719)
reg.cl-ley21719.summary: Chile's comprehensive replacement for the 1999 Law 19.628 regime (see cl-law19628 for the legacy law). Enacted in December 2024 with a 24-month vacatio legis, taking full effect on December 1, 2026. Closely aligned with the GDPR template: introduces a full data-subject-rights catalogue, breach notification, accountability principle, DPIAs for high-risk processing, restrictions on international data transfers, and creates a dedicated Personal Data Protection Agency (Agencia de Proteccion de Datos Personales) with administrative fining powers. A material new compliance surface for any business processing Chilean residents' personal data, including foreign businesses targeting the Chilean market.
reg.cl-ley21719.scope: Applies to the processing of personal data of natural persons in Chile, including extraterritorially to controllers and processors outside Chile that offer goods or services to Chilean residents or monitor their behaviour in Chile. Covers both public and private sector data processing.
reg.cl-ley21719.req.1: Establish a lawful basis for processing (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, legitimate interest balanced against data subject rights, public interest)
reg.cl-ley21719.req.2: Honor data subject rights: access, rectification, deletion, portability, objection, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects
reg.cl-ley21719.req.3: Notify the new Agencia de Proteccion de Datos Personales of personal data breaches within statutory time limits
reg.cl-ley21719.req.4: Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing (large-scale sensitive data, systematic monitoring, automated decision-making)
reg.cl-ley21719.req.5: Appoint a Data Protection Officer where required (public bodies, large-scale sensitive data processing, systematic monitoring)
reg.cl-ley21719.req.6: Restrict international data transfers to jurisdictions without an adequacy declaration unless safeguards (standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, explicit consent) are in place
reg.cl-ley21719.req.7: Maintain processing records demonstrating accountability and respect specific rules for processing sensitive categories of data (health, biometric, genetic, political, religious, sexual life)
reg.cl-ley21719.penalties: Administrative fines tiered by severity. Minor infringements: up to 5,000 UTM (approximately USD 350,000). Serious infringements: up to 10,000 UTM (approximately USD 700,000). Very serious infringements: up to 20,000 UTM (approximately USD 1.4 million) or 4% of annual global turnover, whichever is higher. The Agencia de Proteccion de Datos Personales has investigative and sanctioning powers, replacing the prior court-only enforcement model under Law 19.628.
reg.cn-algo-rec.name: Administrative Provisions on Algorithm Recommendation for Internet Information Services
reg.cn-algo-rec.summary: The world's first comprehensive regulation governing recommendation algorithms. Requires transparency over algorithm functionality, gives users control over their data profiles, and mandates algorithm filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China. Targets services that use algorithms to recommend content to users.
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.1: Algorithm recommendation providers must file algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration of China within 10 working days
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.2: Users must be given the option to disable personalized recommendations
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.3: Algorithms must not be used for anti-competitive practices or price discrimination
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.4: Providers must audit keywords and enable user access to personal data profiles
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.5: Content recommendation algorithms must adhere to mainstream values
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.6: Licensing requirement for providers operating in online news
reg.cn-algo-rec.req.7: Prohibition on algorithmic generation of fake news
reg.cn-algo-rec.penalties: Warnings, public denouncements, rectification orders, administrative fines on companies and individuals, business suspension, and criminal liability for severe violations under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and PIPL.
reg.cn-csl.name: China Cybersecurity Law (CSL)
reg.cn-csl.summary: China's Cybersecurity Law is the foundational legislation governing network security, data protection, and critical information infrastructure in China. It establishes data localization requirements, mandatory security reviews for critical infrastructure operators, and real-name registration for network services, forming the basis of China's broader data governance framework alongside PIPL and the Data Security Law.
reg.cn-csl.req.1: Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) operators must store personal information and important data within China
reg.cn-csl.req.2: Security assessment required for cross-border data transfers by CII operators
reg.cn-csl.req.3: Network operators must implement tiered cybersecurity protection (Multi-Level Protection Scheme)
reg.cn-csl.req.4: Real-name registration required for users of network services
reg.cn-csl.req.5: Mandatory cybersecurity incident reporting and emergency response plans
reg.cn-csl.req.6: Regular network security monitoring, threat detection, and vulnerability management
reg.cn-csl.req.7: Cooperation with public security and national security agencies during investigations
reg.cn-csl.penalties: Fines up to RMB 1 million for network operators and up to RMB 100,000 for directly responsible persons. CII violations can result in fines up to RMB 1 million for the entity and RMB 100,000 for individuals. Business suspension, license revocation, and website closure for serious violations.
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.name: Administrative Provisions on Deep Synthesis in Internet-Based Information Services
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.summary: Regulates the use of deep synthesis (deepfake) technology for generating or altering video, voice, text, and image content online. Requires content labeling, platform responsibilities for blocking harmful content, and establishes mechanisms for algorithm filing and user protection.
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.1: Mandatory labeling and tagging of AI-generated content including voice simulation, face synthesis, and face manipulation
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.2: Establish management systems for algorithm review, ethics review, and content monitoring
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.3: File applicable algorithms with the Cyberspace Administration of China
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.4: Implement personal data protection and child protection measures
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.5: Platform capabilities to identify and block toxic synthesis content
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.6: User reporting mechanisms and timely removal of illegal content
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.req.7: Prohibition on creating politically sensitive deepfake content
reg.cn-deep-synthesis.penalties: Rectification orders, suspension of services, penalties under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and PIPL. Criminal liability for severe violations.
reg.cn-genai.name: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
reg.cn-genai.summary: China's first regulation specifically targeting generative AI services. Governs the provision of text, image, audio, video, and other content generation services to the public within China. Takes a balanced approach promoting innovation while requiring safety assessments and lawful data sourcing.
reg.cn-genai.req.1: Training data must be from lawful sources with no intellectual property infringement
reg.cn-genai.req.2: Obtain consent for personal information used in training
reg.cn-genai.req.3: Ensure training data quality, accuracy, objectivity, and diversity
reg.cn-genai.req.4: Security assessments required for services with public opinion properties or social mobilization capacity
reg.cn-genai.req.6: Generated content must not incite subversion of state power or contain illegal content
reg.cn-genai.req.7: Providers must accept and process user complaints
reg.cn-genai.penalties: Violations penalized under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, PIPL, and Law on Progress of Science and Technology. Includes warnings, rectification orders, and suspension orders.
reg.cn-pipl.name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China
reg.cn-pipl.summary: China's comprehensive personal information protection law, forming a pillar of China's data governance framework alongside the Cybersecurity Law and Data Security Law. It has extraterritorial scope and imposes strict requirements on cross-border data transfers, consent, and data localization.
reg.cn-pipl.req.1: Obtain separate consent for sensitive personal information processing, cross-border transfers, and public disclosure
reg.cn-pipl.req.2: Conduct personal information protection impact assessments for high-risk processing activities
reg.cn-pipl.req.3: Appoint a personal information protection officer and register with authorities
reg.cn-pipl.req.4: Data localization requirements for critical information infrastructure operators and large-scale processors
reg.cn-pipl.req.5: Cross-border data transfer mechanisms: security assessment, standard contracts, or certification
reg.cn-pipl.req.6: Individual rights including access, correction, deletion, portability, and withdrawal of consent
reg.cn-pipl.req.7: Mandatory breach notification to authorities and affected individuals
reg.cn-pipl.penalties: For serious violations: fines up to RMB 50 million (~USD 7 million) or 5% of previous year's annual revenue, suspension or termination of business, revocation of business licenses. Individual liability: fines up to RMB 1 million. Enforced by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC).
reg.co-law1581.name: Law 1581 of 2012 (General Provisions for the Protection of Personal Data)
reg.co-law1581.summary: Colombia's statutory data protection law establishes general provisions for the protection of personal data and habeas data rights. It applies to any processing of personal data in Colombian territory or when Colombian law applies to the data controller.
reg.co-law1581.req.1: Obtain prior, express, and informed authorization (consent) from data subjects
reg.co-law1581.req.2: Register databases with the National Database Registry (RNBD) maintained by the SIC
reg.co-law1581.req.3: Implement a comprehensive data processing policy (privacy policy)
reg.co-law1581.req.4: Appoint a person or department responsible for data protection
reg.co-law1581.req.5: Implement appropriate technical, human, and administrative security measures
reg.co-law1581.req.6: Respect data subject rights (access, update, rectification, deletion, revocation)
reg.co-law1581.req.7: Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection or with consent
reg.co-law1581.penalties: Fines up to 2,000 times the current legal monthly minimum wage (~COP 2.6 billion / ~USD 574,000). Other sanctions include suspension of data processing for up to 6 months, temporary or permanent database closure. Enforced by the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce (SIC).
reg.ec-lopdp.name: Ecuador Organic Law on Personal Data Protection
reg.ec-lopdp.summary: Ecuador's Organic Law on Personal Data Protection is the country's first comprehensive data privacy law, closely modeled on the GDPR. It establishes principles-based data processing rules, individual rights, and cross-border transfer mechanisms, with enforcement by the Data Protection Authority under the Telecommunications Ministry.
reg.ec-lopdp.req.1: Lawful basis for processing including consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, and legitimate interest
reg.ec-lopdp.req.2: Data subject rights including access, rectification, erasure, portability, and objection
reg.ec-lopdp.req.3: Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing
reg.ec-lopdp.req.4: Data Protection Officer appointment for public entities and certain private organizations
reg.ec-lopdp.req.5: Cross-border data transfer restrictions with adequacy or appropriate safeguards requirements
reg.ec-lopdp.req.6: Data breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours
reg.ec-lopdp.penalties: Fines up to 1% of annual turnover for serious violations. Administrative sanctions including temporary or definitive suspension of data processing activities. The Data Protection Authority may conduct audits and issue corrective orders.
reg.eg-pdpl.name: Personal Data Protection Law No. 151 of 2020
reg.eg-pdpl.summary: Egypt's first comprehensive data protection law regulates the processing of personal data by both public and private entities. The Executive Regulations were issued in November 2025 with a 12-month grace period, meaning full enforcement begins approximately November 2026.
reg.eg-pdpl.req.1: Obtain explicit consent before processing personal data
reg.eg-pdpl.req.2: Obtain a license or permit from the Personal Data Protection Center
reg.eg-pdpl.req.3: Notify the PDPC of data breaches within 72 hours, and affected individuals within 3 working days
reg.eg-pdpl.req.4: Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing
reg.eg-pdpl.req.5: Restrict cross-border transfers to PDPC-approved countries with data subject consent
reg.eg-pdpl.penalties: Imprisonment of 3-6 months and fines from EGP 200,000 to EGP 5,000,000 depending on severity. Unauthorized cross-border transfer: minimum 3 months imprisonment and/or EGP 500,000-5,000,000 fine. Enforced by the Personal Data Protection Center (under Ministry of Communications and Information Technology).
reg.eu-ai-act.name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689)
reg.eu-ai-act.summary: The world's first comprehensive AI regulatory framework. Establishes a risk-based classification system for AI systems across the EU, banning certain practices outright and imposing strict requirements on high-risk applications. Applies to providers, deployers, importers, and distributors of AI systems in the EU market, with phased implementation through 2027.
reg.eu-ai-act.req.1: Prohibition of AI for social scoring, subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces
reg.eu-ai-act.req.2: Risk management systems and conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems
reg.eu-ai-act.req.3: High-quality training data requirements with bias detection and mitigation
reg.eu-ai-act.req.4: Transparency obligations including user notification when interacting with AI
reg.eu-ai-act.req.5: Human oversight mechanisms for high-risk AI systems
reg.eu-ai-act.req.6: Registration of high-risk AI systems in an EU-wide public database
reg.eu-ai-act.req.7: General-purpose AI model providers must provide technical documentation, comply with copyright law, and publish training content summaries
reg.eu-ai-act.penalties: Prohibited practices: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global annual turnover. High-risk system violations: up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover. Providing incorrect information: up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% of global annual turnover.
reg.eu-amld6.name: Anti-Money Laundering Directive 6 (AMLD6)
reg.eu-amld6.summary: AMLD6 is the EU's sixth anti-money laundering directive, strengthening the criminal law framework against money laundering across member states. It harmonizes the definition of money laundering predicate offences, extends criminal liability to legal persons, and establishes minimum imprisonment terms to address inconsistencies in enforcement across the EU.
reg.eu-amld6.req.1: Harmonized list of 22 predicate offences for money laundering including cybercrime and environmental crime
reg.eu-amld6.req.2: Criminal liability for legal persons (companies) for money laundering committed for their benefit
reg.eu-amld6.req.3: Minimum imprisonment of 4 years for money laundering offences
reg.eu-amld6.req.4: Extended liability for aiding, abetting, inciting, and attempting money laundering
reg.eu-amld6.req.5: Self-laundering criminalized (laundering proceeds of crimes one committed)
reg.eu-amld6.req.6: Enhanced cooperation between member state Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs)
reg.eu-amld6.penalties: Minimum 4 years imprisonment for natural persons. Legal persons face fines, exclusion from public benefits, judicial winding-up, temporary or permanent closure of establishments. Aggravating circumstances (criminal organization involvement, obliged entity employees) increase penalties.
reg.eu-dora.name: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
reg.eu-dora.summary: DORA is an EU regulation establishing a comprehensive framework for digital operational resilience in the financial sector. It harmonizes ICT risk management, incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing, and third-party risk management rules across all EU financial entities including banks, insurers, investment firms, and their critical ICT service providers.
reg.eu-dora.req.1: ICT risk management framework with governance, identification, protection, detection, response, and recovery capabilities
reg.eu-dora.req.2: Major ICT-related incident reporting to competent authorities within 4 hours (initial), 72 hours (intermediate), and 1 month (final)
reg.eu-dora.req.3: Digital operational resilience testing including threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) every 3 years for significant entities
reg.eu-dora.req.4: Third-party ICT risk management with mandatory contractual provisions for critical service providers
reg.eu-dora.req.5: Oversight framework for critical ICT third-party service providers designated by European Supervisory Authorities
reg.eu-dora.req.6: Information sharing arrangements on cyber threat intelligence between financial entities
reg.eu-dora.penalties: Competent authorities may impose administrative penalties and remedial measures as defined by member state law. Critical ICT third-party service providers face periodic penalty payments of 1% of average daily worldwide turnover. Member states may impose criminal penalties for serious violations.
reg.eu-gdpr.name: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
reg.eu-gdpr.summary: The EU General Data Protection Regulation is the most comprehensive data privacy framework globally. It governs the collection, processing, and storage of personal data for individuals within the European Union, imposing strict consent requirements, data subject rights, and cross-border transfer restrictions.
reg.eu-gdpr.req.1: Lawful basis required for all personal data processing
reg.eu-gdpr.req.2: Explicit consent with clear opt-in mechanisms
reg.eu-gdpr.req.3: Right to access, rectification, erasure, and data portability
reg.eu-gdpr.req.4: Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointment for qualifying organizations
reg.eu-gdpr.req.6: Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) for high-risk processing
reg.eu-gdpr.req.7: Cross-border data transfer safeguards (SCCs, BCRs, adequacy decisions)
reg.eu-gdpr.penalties: Up to 4% of annual global turnover or EUR 20 million, whichever is greater.
reg.eu-mifid2.name: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II)
reg.eu-mifid2.summary: MiFID II is the EU's comprehensive framework for regulating financial markets, investment services, and investor protection. It replaced MiFID I with significantly expanded scope, introducing stricter transparency rules, best execution requirements, product governance obligations, and new trading venue categories to strengthen market integrity across the European Union.
reg.eu-mifid2.req.1: Pre-trade and post-trade transparency requirements for equities, bonds, derivatives, and structured finance products
reg.eu-mifid2.req.2: Best execution obligations with detailed policies, monitoring, and annual reporting to clients
reg.eu-mifid2.req.3: Product governance requirements: manufacturers must define target markets and distribution strategies
reg.eu-mifid2.req.4: Inducements ban for independent advisors; enhanced disclosure for non-independent advice
reg.eu-mifid2.req.5: Transaction reporting to national competent authorities with 65+ data fields within T+1
reg.eu-mifid2.req.6: Algorithmic and high-frequency trading controls including kill switches and risk limits
reg.eu-mifid2.req.7: Third-country firm access through equivalence decisions or member state national regimes
reg.eu-mifid2.penalties: National competent authorities may impose fines of at least EUR 5 million for natural persons and EUR 5 million or 10% of annual turnover for legal persons. Additional sanctions include public censure, withdrawal of authorization, temporary bans on management functions, and disgorgement of profits.
reg.eu-nis2.name: Network and Information Security Directive 2 (NIS2)
reg.eu-nis2.summary: NIS2 is the EU's updated cybersecurity directive replacing the original 2016 NIS Directive. It significantly expands the scope of sectors covered, introduces stricter incident reporting timelines, and imposes personal liability on senior management for cybersecurity failures. Member states were required to transpose it into national law by October 2024.
reg.eu-nis2.req.1: Risk management measures including incident handling, business continuity, and supply chain security
reg.eu-nis2.req.2: 24-hour early warning and 72-hour incident notification to national CSIRTs
reg.eu-nis2.req.3: Senior management accountability and mandatory cybersecurity training for leadership
reg.eu-nis2.req.4: Expanded sector coverage: energy, transport, banking, health, digital infrastructure, ICT service management, public administration, space
reg.eu-nis2.req.5: Supply chain and third-party risk assessment obligations
reg.eu-nis2.req.6: Regular security audits and vulnerability disclosure policies
reg.eu-nis2.req.7: Member state cooperation through EU-CyCLONe crisis management network
reg.eu-nis2.penalties: Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover for essential entities; up to EUR 7 million or 1.4% of turnover for important entities. Personal liability for senior management who fail to ensure compliance.
reg.gb-ai-framework.name: UK Pro-Innovation Approach to AI Regulation (AI Regulation White Paper)
reg.gb-ai-framework.summary: The UK's regulator-led, non-statutory framework for AI governance, set out in the AI Regulation White Paper (March 2023) and the Government's published response (February 2024). Rather than enacting a horizontal AI law (the EU approach), the UK directs existing sector regulators (ICO, CMA, FCA, MHRA, Ofcom, HSE, EHRC) to apply five cross-sectoral principles within their existing remits. Each regulator publishes its own AI strategy; the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) maintains a central AI Safety Institute and a coordination function. Parliament has signaled openness to future statutory backing for the principles (notably for frontier models) but no horizontal AI statute is in force.
reg.gb-ai-framework.scope: Applies to any organization developing or deploying AI systems in the United Kingdom. Specific obligations flow from whichever sector regulator (ICO for data protection, CMA for competition, FCA for financial services, MHRA for medical devices, Ofcom for online safety, etc.) has jurisdiction over the deployment context.
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.1: Safety, Security, and Robustness: AI systems must operate securely and robustly across their lifecycle, with appropriate risk management proportional to context
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.2: Appropriate Transparency and Explainability: organizations must provide stakeholders with sufficient information about AI systems to enable accountable use
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.3: Fairness: AI systems must not undermine legal rights, discriminate unfairly, or produce unfair commercial outcomes
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.4: Accountability and Governance: clear lines of accountability across the AI lifecycle, with effective oversight by the deploying organization
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.5: Contestability and Redress: affected parties must be able to challenge AI-driven decisions and seek redress where harm occurs
reg.gb-ai-framework.req.6: Engage with the relevant sector regulator's published AI guidance (ICO AI and data protection guidance, FCA AI in financial services framework, MHRA Software and AI as a Medical Device, etc.) as the operational compliance baseline
reg.gb-dpa.name: UK Data Protection Act 2018
reg.gb-dpa.summary: The UK Data Protection Act 2018 supplements the UK GDPR (retained EU law post-Brexit) and provides a comprehensive data protection framework. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is the independent supervisory authority responsible for enforcement.
reg.gb-dpa.req.1: Lawful basis required for processing personal data (mirrors UK GDPR)
reg.gb-dpa.req.2: Enhanced protections for special category and criminal conviction data
reg.gb-dpa.req.3: Rights of data subjects including access, rectification, and erasure
reg.gb-dpa.req.4: Data Protection Officer required for public authorities and high-risk processing
reg.gb-dpa.req.5: International data transfer mechanisms (UK adequacy regulations, SCCs)
reg.gb-dpa.req.6: Mandatory breach notification to ICO within 72 hours
reg.gb-dpa.req.7: Age-appropriate design code for children's online services
reg.gb-dpa.penalties: Up to GBP 17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover, whichever is greater.
reg.gb-fsma.name: Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (FSMA 2023)
reg.gb-fsma.summary: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 is the UK's post-Brexit overhaul of financial services regulation. It revokes retained EU financial services law, transfers regulatory powers to the FCA and PRA, introduces a new framework for crypto-asset regulation, and establishes secondary competitiveness and growth objectives for UK financial regulators.
reg.gb-fsma.req.1: Revocation of retained EU financial services law and transfer of rulemaking to FCA and PRA
reg.gb-fsma.req.2: Designated Activities Regime (DAR) for regulating specific financial activities outside traditional authorization
reg.gb-fsma.req.3: Crypto-asset regulation framework bringing stablecoins and broader crypto activities under FCA oversight
reg.gb-fsma.req.4: Secondary objectives for FCA and PRA to facilitate international competitiveness and medium-term growth
reg.gb-fsma.req.5: Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR) extension and accountability framework
reg.gb-fsma.req.6: Access to cash: requirements to maintain reasonable provision of cash access services
reg.gb-fsma.penalties: FCA and PRA enforcement powers including unlimited fines for market abuse and regulatory breaches. Criminal penalties for unauthorized financial activities up to 2 years imprisonment. Public censure, prohibition orders, and restitution orders.
reg.gb-nis.name: UK Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 (NIS Regulations)
reg.gb-nis.summary: The UK NIS Regulations implement the EU NIS Directive into UK law and remain in force post-Brexit. They impose cybersecurity and incident reporting obligations on operators of essential services and relevant digital service providers across critical sectors including energy, transport, health, water, and digital infrastructure.
reg.gb-nis.req.1: Operators of Essential Services (OES) must take appropriate and proportionate security measures
reg.gb-nis.req.2: Mandatory incident notification to relevant competent authorities without undue delay
reg.gb-nis.req.3: Implementation of the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) principles
reg.gb-nis.req.4: Relevant Digital Service Providers must ensure security of network and information systems
reg.gb-nis.req.5: Competent authorities designated per sector (Ofgem for energy, Ofcom for digital infrastructure, etc.)
reg.gb-nis.req.6: Regular risk assessments and implementation of security measures proportionate to identified risks
reg.gb-nis.penalties: Fines up to GBP 17 million for failure to implement appropriate security measures or report incidents. Enforcement notices, penalty notices, and information requests by competent authorities. NCSC provides technical guidance but enforcement is sector-specific.
reg.gh-dpa.name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)
reg.gh-dpa.summary: Ghana's Data Protection Act was one of the earliest comprehensive data protection laws in Africa. It establishes the Data Protection Commission, regulates the processing of personal data by both public and private entities, and sets conditions for lawful processing, individual rights, and cross-border data transfers.
reg.gh-dpa.req.1: Registration with the Data Protection Commission before processing personal data
reg.gh-dpa.req.2: Consent or other lawful basis required for processing personal data
reg.gh-dpa.req.3: Data subjects' rights to access, correction, and deletion of personal data
reg.gh-dpa.req.4: Data Protection Commission oversight with investigation and enforcement powers
reg.gh-dpa.req.5: Cross-border data transfers only to countries with adequate data protection
reg.gh-dpa.req.6: Special protections for sensitive personal data including health, political opinions, and religious beliefs
reg.gh-dpa.penalties: Fines of up to GHS 36,000 (250 penalty units) for failure to register. Administrative sanctions including compliance orders and suspension of data processing activities. Criminal penalties for unlawful data processing.
reg.global-basel3.name: Basel III International Banking Standards
reg.global-basel3.summary: Basel III is a comprehensive set of international banking standards developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision to strengthen regulation, supervision, and risk management of banks worldwide. Finalized after the 2008 financial crisis, it sets minimum requirements for capital adequacy, leverage ratios, and liquidity, with full implementation phased through 2028.
reg.global-basel3.req.1: Minimum Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of 4.5% plus capital conservation buffer of 2.5%
reg.global-basel3.req.2: Leverage ratio minimum of 3% to constrain excessive balance sheet growth
reg.global-basel3.req.3: Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): sufficient high-quality liquid assets to cover 30-day net cash outflows
reg.global-basel3.req.4: Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR): stable funding relative to liquidity profiles of assets over one year
reg.global-basel3.req.5: Countercyclical capital buffer of 0-2.5% set by national authorities based on credit conditions
reg.global-basel3.req.6: Standardized approach for credit risk with revised risk weight framework
reg.global-basel3.req.7: Output floor: internal model capital requirements cannot fall below 72.5% of standardized approach
reg.global-basel3.penalties: Basel III is implemented through national legislation; penalties vary by jurisdiction. Non-compliant banks face supervisory actions including capital surcharges, restrictions on dividends and bonus payments, enhanced reporting requirements, and potential revocation of banking licenses.
reg.global-pci-dss.name: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)
reg.global-pci-dss.summary: PCI DSS is a global information security standard established by the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC), founded by Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, and JCB. It is not a government law but an industry standard enforced contractually by card networks and acquiring banks. Organizations that fail to comply risk fines, increased transaction fees, and loss of card processing privileges.
reg.global-pci-dss.scope: Any organization that stores, processes, or transmits payment cardholder data, including merchants, payment processors, acquirers, issuers, and service providers
reg.global-pci-dss.req.1: Install and maintain network security controls (firewalls, network segmentation)
reg.global-pci-dss.req.2: Apply secure configurations to all system components
reg.global-pci-dss.req.3: Protect stored account data with encryption and access controls
reg.global-pci-dss.req.4: Encrypt transmission of cardholder data across open, public networks
reg.global-pci-dss.req.5: Protect all systems and networks from malicious software
reg.global-pci-dss.req.6: Develop and maintain secure systems and software
reg.global-pci-dss.req.7: Restrict access to system components and cardholder data by business need-to-know
reg.global-pci-dss.req.8: Identify users and authenticate access to system components
reg.global-pci-dss.req.9: Restrict physical access to cardholder data
reg.global-pci-dss.req.10: Log and monitor all access to system components and cardholder data
reg.global-pci-dss.req.11: Test security of systems and networks regularly
reg.global-pci-dss.req.12: Support information security with organizational policies and programs
reg.global-pci-dss.penalties: Non-compliance penalties are contractual, not statutory. Card networks may impose fines of $5,000 to $100,000 per month on acquiring banks, which pass costs to merchants. Severe non-compliance can result in increased transaction fees, mandatory forensic audits, and revocation of card processing privileges.
reg.id-pdp.name: Personal Data Protection Law (Law No. 27 of 2022)
reg.id-pdp.summary: Indonesia's first comprehensive personal data protection law, enacted October 2022 with a two-year transition period making it fully enforceable from 17 October 2024. It covers both electronic and non-electronic personal data processing and applies to entities within and outside Indonesia processing data of Indonesian residents.
reg.id-pdp.req.1: Obtain valid and explicit consent for personal data processing
reg.id-pdp.req.2: Mandatory breach notification to data subjects within 72 hours of discovering a breach
reg.id-pdp.req.3: Data subject rights including access, correction, deletion, portability, and withdrawal of consent
reg.id-pdp.req.4: Conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing
reg.id-pdp.req.5: Appoint a Data Protection Officer for large-scale processing or sensitive data
reg.id-pdp.req.6: Cross-border data transfer restrictions requiring equivalent protection in receiving country
reg.id-pdp.req.7: Maintain records of data processing activities
reg.id-pdp.penalties: Administrative fines up to 2% of annual revenue. Criminal penalties: imprisonment up to 4-6 years and/or fines up to IDR 4-6 billion (~USD 250,000-400,000). For corporations, monetary penalties can be up to 10x the individual maximum. Enforced by the Ministry of Communications and Digital (interim, pending establishment of dedicated DPA).
reg.il-cnda.name: Israel Cyber Network Defense Act
reg.il-cnda.summary: Israel's Cyber Network Defense Act formalizes the Israel National Cyber Directorate's (INCD) authority to protect civilian cyberspace and critical infrastructure. It establishes legal powers for threat detection, incident response, and mandatory reporting, positioning Israel's cybersecurity framework among the most operationally active globally.
reg.il-cnda.req.1: Israel National Cyber Directorate (INCD) authority over civilian cybersecurity defense
reg.il-cnda.req.2: Mandatory cybersecurity incident reporting for designated essential service organizations
reg.il-cnda.req.3: Real-time threat intelligence sharing between INCD and critical infrastructure operators
reg.il-cnda.req.4: INCD authority to issue binding cybersecurity directives during active cyber threats
reg.il-cnda.req.5: Cybersecurity standards and guidelines for essential service sectors
reg.il-cnda.req.6: National CERT (CERT-IL) coordination for civilian incident response and threat mitigation
reg.il-cnda.penalties: Non-compliance with INCD directives may result in administrative enforcement measures and regulatory sanctions. Essential service organizations face corrective orders and mandatory remediation. Criminal penalties for cybercrimes addressed under existing computer crime statutes.
reg.il-ppl.name: Israel Privacy Protection Law (Amendment 13)
reg.il-ppl.summary: Israel's Privacy Protection Law, significantly strengthened by Amendment 13, regulates the collection, storage, use, and transfer of personal data. Israel holds an EU adequacy decision enabling cross-border data transfers. The amendment modernized breach notification requirements, strengthened the Privacy Protection Authority's enforcement powers, and increased penalties.
reg.il-ppl.req.1: Database registration with the Privacy Protection Authority for databases exceeding defined thresholds
reg.il-ppl.req.2: Purpose limitation: personal data may only be used for the purpose for which it was collected
reg.il-ppl.req.3: Data security obligations proportionate to the type and sensitivity of data processed
reg.il-ppl.req.4: Mandatory breach notification to the Privacy Protection Authority and affected individuals
reg.il-ppl.req.5: Cross-border data transfer restrictions with adequacy-based exceptions
reg.il-ppl.req.6: Individual rights to access, correction, and deletion of personal data
reg.il-ppl.penalties: Administrative fines up to ILS 3.2 million per violation following Amendment 13. Criminal penalties including imprisonment for unauthorized use of personal data. The Privacy Protection Authority has expanded enforcement and investigation powers.
reg.in-cert.name: CERT-In Cybersecurity Directions
reg.in-cert.summary: India's CERT-In Directions issued under the Information Technology Act mandate strict cybersecurity incident reporting and data retention requirements for all organizations operating in India. The directions require reporting of cybersecurity incidents within 6 hours and impose log retention obligations of 180 days within Indian jurisdiction.
reg.in-cert.req.1: Report cybersecurity incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing or being notified
reg.in-cert.req.2: Maintain ICT system logs for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction
reg.in-cert.req.3: Synchronize ICT system clocks to Network Time Protocol (NTP) servers
reg.in-cert.req.4: Data centres, VPS providers, cloud providers, and VPN providers must register subscriber information for 5 years
reg.in-cert.req.5: Virtual asset service providers must maintain KYC and transaction records for 5 years
reg.in-cert.req.6: Designate a Point of Contact for CERT-In communications
reg.in-cert.penalties: Non-compliance may result in imprisonment up to one year or fine up to INR 100,000 under the IT Act. CERT-In may issue directions to block, restrict, or mandate specific security measures. Service providers may face license revocation.
reg.in-dpdpa.name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
reg.in-dpdpa.summary: India's first comprehensive digital personal data protection law. It regulates the processing of digital personal data within India and cross-border processing of Indian citizens' data. Enforcement is phased, with full consent and processing obligations taking effect by May 2027.
reg.in-dpdpa.req.1: Obtain free, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent with clear privacy notices
reg.in-dpdpa.req.2: Mandatory data breach notification to the Data Protection Board and affected individuals
reg.in-dpdpa.req.3: Data principals have rights to access, correction, erasure, and grievance redressal
reg.in-dpdpa.req.4: Heightened protections for children's data including verifiable parental consent
reg.in-dpdpa.req.5: Data fiduciaries must implement reasonable security safeguards
reg.in-dpdpa.req.6: Restrictions on cross-border data transfers to notified countries
reg.in-dpdpa.penalties: Maximum penalty of INR 250 crore (~USD 30 million) per contravention. Specific penalties: up to INR 200 crore for failure to notify breaches, up to INR 200 crore for children's data violations. Enforced by the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI).
reg.jp-ai-promotion.name: Act on the Promotion of Research and Development and the Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (AI Promotion Act)
reg.jp-ai-promotion.summary: Japan's first comprehensive AI legislation, structured as a fundamental law establishing high-level principles rather than prescriptive rules. Embodies Japan's agile governance philosophy, positioning the country to be the most AI-friendly nation while promoting responsible AI development and use.
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.1: Enhance AI research and development capabilities
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.3: Promote international cooperation on AI governance
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.4: Businesses and citizens to cooperate with government on reasonable efforts basis
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.5: Establish AI Strategy Headquarters under the Prime Minister's Office
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.6: Government may issue advice and guidance to businesses using AI harmfully
reg.jp-ai-promotion.req.7: Promote comprehensive stakeholder initiatives from R&D to social implementation
reg.jp-ai-promotion.penalties: No direct fines or penalties. Authorities may issue advice, request information, or publicly disclose non-compliance. Enforcement relies on existing sector-specific laws including privacy, competition, intellectual property, and product safety.
reg.jp-apcs.name: Act on the Protection of Critical Infrastructure Services (Japan)
reg.jp-apcs.summary: Japan's updated critical infrastructure protection framework strengthens cybersecurity obligations for operators across 14 critical sectors. Building on the Basic Act on Cybersecurity and NISC guidelines, it mandates incident reporting, risk assessments, and coordination with the National Center of Incident Readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity (NISC).
reg.jp-apcs.req.1: Mandatory cybersecurity incident reporting to sector-specific regulators and NISC
reg.jp-apcs.req.2: Implementation of cybersecurity risk management measures aligned with NISC guidelines
reg.jp-apcs.req.3: Covers 14 critical sectors including information and communications, finance, aviation, railways, electric power, gas, government services, healthcare, water, and logistics
reg.jp-apcs.req.4: Business continuity planning and disaster recovery for cyber incidents
reg.jp-apcs.req.5: Supply chain cybersecurity risk management obligations
reg.jp-apcs.req.6: Coordination with NISC for cross-sector incident response
reg.jp-apcs.penalties: Administrative guidance and corrective orders from sector-specific regulators. Public disclosure of non-compliant operators. Regulatory penalties vary by sector-specific implementing legislation.
reg.jp-appi.name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI)
reg.jp-appi.summary: Japan's comprehensive data protection law, significantly amended in 2020 with changes taking effect April 2022. It regulates how businesses handle personal information, with extraterritorial reach covering foreign entities processing data of individuals in Japan.
reg.jp-appi.req.1: Obtain consent before providing personal data to third parties
reg.jp-appi.req.2: Mandatory breach notification to the PPC and affected individuals for qualifying incidents
reg.jp-appi.req.3: Restrictions on cross-border data transfers requiring consent or equivalent protection
reg.jp-appi.req.4: Individual rights including access, correction, deletion, and usage suspension
reg.jp-appi.req.5: Obligation to specify and publicly announce the purpose of use of personal information
reg.jp-appi.req.6: Appoint a personal information protection manager
reg.jp-appi.req.7: Maintain records of third-party data transfers and receipts
reg.jp-appi.penalties: No administrative fines. Criminal penalties: up to JPY 100 million (~USD 680,000) for corporations and up to JPY 1 million and/or 1 year imprisonment for individuals who violate PPC orders. Enforced by the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC).
reg.ke-cmca.name: Kenya Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018
reg.ke-cmca.summary: Kenya's Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act provides the legal framework for cybersecurity offences, critical infrastructure protection, and international cooperation on cybercrimes. It establishes the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4) and Kenya Computer Incident Response Team (KE-CIRT) for coordinating cybersecurity incident response.
reg.ke-cmca.req.1: National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4) for policy coordination and oversight
reg.ke-cmca.req.2: Kenya Computer Incident Response Team (KE-CIRT) for national incident detection and response
reg.ke-cmca.req.3: Critical infrastructure designation and protection obligations
reg.ke-cmca.req.4: Mandatory cybersecurity incident reporting for service providers and critical infrastructure operators
reg.ke-cmca.req.5: Criminalization of unauthorized access, interference with computer systems, and cyber espionage
reg.ke-cmca.req.6: International mutual assistance and cooperation on cybercrime investigations
reg.ke-cmca.penalties: Fines up to KES 20 million and/or imprisonment up to 20 years for critical infrastructure attacks. Unauthorized access penalties of up to KES 5 million and/or 3 years imprisonment. False publication offences carry fines up to KES 5 million and/or 2 years imprisonment.
reg.ke-dpa.name: Data Protection Act, No. 24 of 2019
reg.ke-dpa.summary: Kenya's Data Protection Act establishes a comprehensive framework for the protection of personal data, applying to all organizations that collect, process, or store personal data of individuals in Kenya. It created the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) as the regulatory authority.
reg.ke-dpa.req.1: Register as a data controller or processor with the Data Commissioner
reg.ke-dpa.req.2: Obtain consent before collecting or processing personal data
reg.ke-dpa.req.3: Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing
reg.ke-dpa.req.4: Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
reg.ke-dpa.req.5: Notify the Data Commissioner of data breaches within 72 hours
reg.ke-dpa.req.6: Appoint a Data Protection Officer where required
